1.text: Relatives by affinity are called collectively mataˊlit (pl.) or mataˊlɪ-raˊmkɪn

3.text: Men married to two sisters call each other takaˊlhɪn. Takaˊlhɪn more

4.text: properly signifies “brace-companion;” for instance, one of the two reindeer

5.text: harnessed to the sledge. Pɪtkaˊ-takaˊlhɪn signifies “twin-brother” (literally,

6.text: “double-companion”). The degree of affinity thus indicated is considered to

7.text: be very strong. In olden times it was considered even stronger than brother-

8.text: hood. Takaˊlhɪn kɪrñaˊ-yêˊčamêt-tɵmg̣êˊpu paˊroč signifies “man of the wife’s

9.text: sister (is) of the old-male-brother beyond.” An old proverb says, “Man of

10.text: the wife’s sister is on the same lake shore a fall-companion” (takaˊlhɪn ᴇnnaˊn-

11.text: hɪˊthɪlɪñkɪ rɪlteˊl-tɵˊmg̣ɪn). This means that both are to fight and fall together.

12.text: The Chukchee say that if one takaˊlhɪn sees the blood of the other drawn

13.text: by an enemy, he will rush forward again and again until his own body lies

14.text: on the same spot. Perhaps this relation may be considered as a survival of

15.text: group-marriage, although at present group-marriage between the takaˊlhɪt

16.text: exists but rarely. The group-marriage, and the degree of relationship based

17.text: on it, will be described later on.

19.text: The family is designated as raˊyɪrɪn (“houseful,” or simply “those in the

20.text: house”), yaraˊ-tɵˊmgɪt (“house-mates”); but both these terms relate, properly

21.text: speaking, to the house and those living in it. The house with those living

22.text: in it forms the real basis of the Chukchee family. Members of the family

23.text: who have left the house (or, among the Reindeer Chukchee, the camp) lose

24.text: their connection with the household and also with the family.
